newsitem.title: UK: UK global trade deficit slashed as exports soar.
newsitem.headline: UK global trade deficit slashed as exports soar.

text.p: Britain's trade deficit with the rest of the world narrowed sharply in October as exports were snapped up, official figures showed.
Britain's trade deficit was pared to 454 million pounds ($760.1 million) in October from 1,059 million in September, the Office for National Statistics said on Tuesday.
But more up-to-date figures for Britain's trade with non-European Union nations showed a deficit of 639 million pounds in November, well above October's 418 million shortfall.
Treasury minister Phillip Oppenheim welcomed the figures and said they showed UK exports were on a strong upward path.
Britain exported goods worth 14.62 billion pounds to the rest of the world in October. In September, total exports were just below 14 billion.
"These figures again show that growth is broadly balanced and illustrate the growing success of the British economy," Oppenheim said.
The ONS said the erratic pattern of trade figures made a trend difficult to discern. But it said its latest estimate suggested the global trade gap was narrowing.
Economists said the trade gap could narrow further in the short term as sterling's powerful rally cuts import prices.

Lower import prices will result in a fall in the total value of goods imported even if imported volumes rise, the so-called "J-curve" effect. On the other side of the equation, the pound's strength has pushed up export prices, thus increasing the value of exports.

"The trade deficit is benefiting from a textbook "J-curve" effect as sterling's rise has pushed exports up and import prices down, but volumes have yet to react," said Jonathan Loynes, UK economist at HSBC Markets.

But that effect is unlikely to be sustained in the longer term. "Further out, firmer domestic demand and the squeeze on export growth will result in a wider deficit in 1997," said Philip Shaw, chief economist at Union Plc.

Most major European economies are still weak, so higher British export prices are bound to depress volumes after a while. Also, the increasingly spendthrift British consumer is bound to buy more imported goods if spending remains at its current rate.
The pound has risen about 12 percent against a basket of major currencies since early August.

Andrew Milligan, economist at General Accident, agreed exports were holding up well despite the pound's stellar performance. But he noted the last Confederation of British Industry trends survey showed UK manufacturers were starting to report a marked fall in export orders.

Of about 1,200 manufacturing firms surveyed by the CBI in December, 15 percent more said export order books had shrunk than said orders had risen. In November, reports of falling orders outweighed rises by only five percent.
But compared with the 1980s, when Britain's current account deficit swelled to gargantuan proportions, its trade position now is unlikely to threaten the economy even if the deficit does widen again.
"The current account is not nearly as bad as it was in the early 1980s, it's not far off balance," said Shaw. "The trade position poses no threat to the health of the economy."
As for the widening trade gap with non-EU countries, Shaw noted that trade statistics are notoriously erratic. "You really can't read too much into one month's set of data." ($1=.5973 Pound)
